title: Pair production and annihilation; Fission and reactors

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Rest energy
items.clue: Quantity linked to mass that becomes photons: 0.511 MeV for one electron.

items.label: Positron
items.clue: Written e⁺: it meets an electron at low speed to give two 0.511 MeV gamma photons.

items.label: Antiparticle
items.clue: General name for a counterpart with the same mass but opposite charge; every type has one.

items.label: Annihilation
items.clue: Event in which matter meets its opposite counterpart and both turn into photons, usually two.

questions.stem: Some very heavy nuclides, such as californium-252, can undergo spontaneous fission, whereas uranium-235 in a reactor undergoes neutron-induced fission. Which statement about spontaneous fission is correct?

options.text: Energy is released as kinetic energy of an α particle that breaks off the nucleus.
Energy is released only once the material is hot enough for its nuclei to shake apart.
No energy is released, as no neutron has been absorbed to supply the energy.
Energy is released when the nucleus splits into two fragments of comparable mass.

questions.stem: An electron and a positron annihilate, producing two photons. Which quantity is different after the annihilation from before it?
questions.explanation: Photons have no rest mass. The pair's mass has been converted to photon energy, but energy and momentum are conserved.

questions.stem: A uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron and splits into two fragments and 2 free neutrons. The fragments contain 234 nucleons in total. The binding energy per nucleon is 7.6 MeV for uranium-235 and about 8.5 MeV for the fragments. A free neutron has no binding energy. Roughly how much energy is released?
questions.explanation: Energy released = increase in total binding energy = 234 × 8.5 − 235 × 7.6 = 1989 − 1786 ≈ 200 MeV.

questions.stem: A muon and an antimuon, both almost at rest, annihilate to produce two photons. The rest energy of a muon is 105.7 MeV. What is the wavelength of each photon?

In a reactor core, each fission of uranium-235 releases 2.5 neutrons on average. Of these, on average 0.7 escape from the core and 0.8 are absorbed by the control rods and other materials without causing fission. What happens to the rate of fission?

options.text: It increases: each fission releases more neutrons than the one it absorbed.
It stays constant: on average one neutron per fission causes a fission.
It decreases: control rods absorb neutrons and so shut the reaction down.
It increases: the energy released heats the fuel, so that more nuclei split.

questions.stem: A photon creates a proton–antiproton pair. The mass of a proton is 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. What is the minimum frequency of the photon?

Predict first. In a gas-cooled reactor, the uranium fuel rods sit in channels through a large block of graphite, which is the moderator. Carbon dioxide gas carries thermal energy from the core. What is the role of the graphite?

options.text: It slows fast neutrons by collisions, as slow neutrons are more likely to cause fission.
It absorbs surplus neutrons from the fuel, so that the rate of fission is kept under control.
It speeds up the neutrons so that they hit uranium nuclei hard enough to split them.
It moderates the temperature of the core, stopping the fuel from overheating.

questions.stem: An electron and a positron, each with 0.30 MeV of kinetic energy, collide head-on and annihilate into two photons. The rest energy of an electron is 0.511 MeV. What is the energy of each photon?
questions.explanation: Head-on with equal energies, the total momentum is zero, so the two photons have equal energies and fly apart in opposite directions. Each: 0.511 + 0.30 = 0.81 MeV.

questions.stem: High-level waste from a reactor contains caesium-137, a fission product with a half-life of 30 years. The waste is kept in a store for 90 years. What percentage of the initial caesium-137 activity remains at the end of this time?
